# Summary

**Background.** Ebola outbreaks can disrupt access to care for other conditions, yet routine surveillance rarely separates this from reporting failure in real time. We assessed whether notified routine morbidity fell more in health zones with greater Ebola virus disease (EVD) burden during the 2026 outbreak in Ituri, DR Congo.

**Methods.** We did a controlled interrupted time series using weekly Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response data from all `r nrow(expo)` Ituri health zones, weeks 1–`r SF` of 2026. Exposure was cumulative confirmed EVD incidence per 10,000 at national situation report `r cfg$epidemie$sitrep_exposition`. We fitted Poisson pseudo-likelihood models with zone and week fixed effects for five high-volume syndromes, estimating ratios of rate ratios (RRR) comparing the period from week `r cfg$epidemie$semaine_rupture` with the earlier period, for a zone with 10 EVD cases per 10,000 versus none. Inference used zone-clustered standard errors and permutation tests with Holm adjustment.

**Findings.** Of `r nrow(expo)` zones, `r sum(expo$mve > 0)` had confirmed EVD cases. Acute respiratory infection notifications had an RRR of `r ci(res[["IRA"]]$principal)`, with no evidence of differential pre-outbreak trends; pneumonia `r ci(res[["PNEUMONIE"]]$principal)`, typhoid fever `r ci(res[["FIEVRE TYPHOIDE"]]$principal)` and suspected malaria `r ci(res[["PALUDISME SUSP"]]$principal)`, although the suspected malaria estimate failed a placebo test and is likely overstated. Diarrhoea with dehydration in children under 5 years was `r ci(res[["DIARRHEE DHY M5"]]$principal)`. Separately, `r nrow(rupt)` zones, including `r sum(rupt$zs %in% expo$zs[expo$mve == 0])` without EVD, showed an abrupt loss of confirmed malaria reporting while suspected notifications persisted, which accounted for most of the apparent province-wide fall in malaria positivity.

**Interpretation.** Notified routine morbidity declined more where EVD burden was greater, consistent with reduced care-seeking, service disruption, or reporting loss, which these data cannot separate. Without 2025 data, season cannot be fully excluded. Province-level malaria trends during this outbreak should not be read as changes in transmission without testing-stock data.

# Introduction

The 2014–16 West African Ebola epidemic showed that the burden of an outbreak extends well beyond Ebola cases. Health-care utilisation fell across affected countries, and modelling suggested substantial excess morbidity and mortality from malaria and other conditions as services were disrupted [@brolin2016; @elston2017; @walker2015; @parpia2016].

An EVD outbreak was declared in Ituri on 15 May 2026 (week `r cfg$epidemie$semaine_rupture`). By situation report `r cfg$epidemie$sitrep_exposition` (14 August 2026), `r sum(expo$mve > 0)` of `r nrow(expo)` health zones had confirmed cases, with burden varying widely between zones. This variation, combined with weekly surveillance data covering the months before the declaration, offers an opportunity to assess indirect effects within one province while conditioning on shared shocks.

Routine surveillance also has a particular weakness during emergencies: a fall in notifications can reflect less disease, less care-seeking, fewer tests, or fewer reports. We therefore aimed to estimate the association between local EVD burden and change in notified routine morbidity, and to characterise the data artefacts that could be mistaken for epidemiological trends.

# Methods

## Study design and data sources

We did a controlled interrupted time series with a continuous exposure [@lopezbernal2017; @lopezbernal2018], reported according to STROBE and RECORD [@vonelm2007; @benchimol2015]. The unit of analysis was the health-zone week. Weekly case and death counts by zone and syndrome came from the Provincial Health Division (DPS) Ituri surveillance database. Cumulative confirmed EVD cases by zone came from national situation report `r cfg$epidemie$sitrep_exposition`, transcribed from the secondary source listed in the supplementary appendix.

## Outcomes

Primary outcomes, chosen as the high-volume syndromes reported consistently across zones, were notifications of `r paste(tolower(lab(prim)), collapse = "; ")`. Secondary outcomes were confirmed malaria, the ratio of confirmed to suspected malaria, and weekly report submission. The number of patients tested is not recorded; the confirmed-to-suspected ratio is therefore a proxy for test positivity. Deaths were too few for modelling and are described only.

## Exposure

Exposure was $\log(1+I)$, where $I$ is cumulative confirmed EVD incidence per 10,000 population. Estimates are expressed for a contrast of `r a$incidence_reference` per 10,000 versus none. The exposure is fixed at a single date within the post-period because weekly zone-level series were unavailable to us.

## Data processing

The raw file was never edited. Scripted rules, each logged with its count (appendix), removed `r ligne_journal(ids, "Rows without")` empty rows and `r ligne_journal(ids, "Exact duplicate")` exact duplicates; resolved `r ligne_journal(ids, "Conflicting")` conflicting zone-week-syndrome records by keeping the highest value (alternatives tested); recomputed `r ligne_journal(ids, "Week-start")` inconsistent week-start dates; and replaced two denominators present per zone with one. A zone-week without any report was treated as missing. Within a submitted report, an absent row was treated as zero, unless the zone's median for that syndrome was at least `r cfg$nettoyage$mediane_zone_pour_zero`, in which case a zero or absent row was treated as missing.

A loss of malaria confirmation was defined as the first of at least `r cfg$paludisme$min_sous_seuil` of `r cfg$paludisme$fenetre` reported weeks with a confirmed-to-suspected ratio below `r 100 * cfg$paludisme$positivite_rupture`% in a zone whose pre-outbreak median was at least `r 100 * cfg$paludisme$positivite_base_min`%. Confirmed malaria was set to missing from that week. Zones where confirmed equalled suspected counts in at least half of pre-outbreak weeks were also excluded from confirmed malaria analyses.

## Statistical analysis

For each outcome we fitted

$$\log \mathrm{E}[Y_{it}] = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \beta \,(\mathrm{Post}_t \times D_i),$$

where $\alpha_i$ and $\gamma_t$ are zone and week fixed effects, $\mathrm{Post}_t$ indicates week `r cfg$epidemie$semaine_rupture` onward and $D_i$ is the exposure. Week effects absorb any province-wide shock or seasonal pattern shared across zones; zone effects absorb time-invariant differences, including population, which is why denominator errors do not affect these estimates. Poisson pseudo-likelihood is consistent under arbitrary overdispersion if the mean is correctly specified. The exposure has a common start, so staggered-adoption bias [@goodmanbacon2021] does not arise in the main specification.

Confidence intervals used zone-clustered standard errors and a *t*(`r nrow(expo) - 1`) reference. We also computed permutation *P* values by reassigning exposure among zones (`r n_en(R$n_perm)` permutations), and applied Holm adjustment across the five primary outcomes. Absolute differences were estimated as the implied counterfactual minus observed notifications in exposed zones, over observed weeks.

We assessed pre-outbreak differential trends with an event study in 4-week bins (reference: weeks 16–19) and a joint Wald test, and a placebo break at week `r a$semaine_placebo` using pre-outbreak data only. Sensitivity analyses comprised: case-count and surveillance-based exposures; categorical exposure; zone-specific linear trends; excluding the two highest-burden zones, weeks 20–21, or zones reporting under `r 100 * a$couverture_min_zone`% of weeks; alternative duplicate rules; removing one zone at a time; and a negative binomial generalised additive mixed model with a smooth for week, random zone intercepts and a population offset, checked with randomised quantile residuals [@dunn1996].

All analyses used R `r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".")`. Code, a locked package list and automated tests are in the replication package. The analysis plan was finalised after initial data exploration and was not registered; results should be treated as hypothesis-generating until replicated.

# Results

The source file contained `r n_en(ids$n_brut)` rows. Of `r n_en(nrow(expo) * SF)` expected zone-weeks, `r n_en(dplyr::n_distinct(paste(ids$donnees$zs, ids$donnees$semaine)))` (`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dplyr::n_distinct(paste(ids$donnees$zs, ids$donnees$semaine)) / (nrow(expo) * SF))`%) had a submitted report. Report submission fell most in higher-burden zones, from `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * R$rapportage_groupes$r[R$rapportage_groupes$groupe == "Higher" & R$rapportage_groupes$post == 0])`% to `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * R$rapportage_groupes$r[R$rapportage_groupes$groupe == "Higher" & R$rapportage_groupes$post == 1])`%, compared with `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * R$rapportage_groupes$r[R$rapportage_groupes$groupe == "None" & R$rapportage_groupes$post == 0])`% to `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * R$rapportage_groupes$r[R$rapportage_groupes$groupe == "None" & R$rapportage_groupes$post == 1])`% in zones without EVD, although the dose-response estimate for 10 per 10,000 was imprecise (`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * R$rapportage$dif)` percentage points, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * R$rapportage$bas)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * R$rapportage$haut)`). Table 1 describes zones by EVD burden. Notifications of acute haemorrhagic fever began to rise in week 20 (figure 1).

## Loss of malaria confirmation

Province-wide, the confirmed-to-suspected ratio fell from `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(pos_prov$brute[pos_prov$semaine < cfg$epidemie$semaine_rupture]))`% before the outbreak to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pos_prov$brute[pos_prov$semaine == SF])`% in week `r SF`. This fall was not evenly distributed (figure 2). In `r nrow(rupt)` zones confirmed counts collapsed abruptly, while suspected notifications persisted; onset ranged from week `r min(rupt$debut_rupture)` to week `r max(rupt$debut_rupture)`, and `r sum(rupt$zs %in% expo$zs[expo$mve == 0])` of these zones had no confirmed EVD. Excluding affected zone-weeks, the ratio was `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pos_prov$corrigee[pos_prov$semaine == SF])`% in week `r SF`. The pattern is what a rapid diagnostic test stock-out or a stop in reporting of confirmed cases would produce, but stock data were not available to test this.

Dashed line: week of outbreak declaration."}

  geom_segment(data = mar, aes(x = debut_rupture - 0.5, xend = debut_rupture - 0.5, y = as.numeric(z) - 0.45, yend = as.numeric(z) + 0.45),

        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7.5), legend.key.width = grid::unit(28, "pt"))

## Association with EVD burden

Associations are in table 2. All five primary outcomes had point estimates below 1. After Holm adjustment, *P* was `r pv(res[["PALUDISME SUSP"]]$principal$p_holm)` for suspected malaria, `r pv(res[["IRA"]]$principal$p_holm)` for acute respiratory infection, `r pv(res[["PNEUMONIE"]]$principal$p_holm)` for pneumonia, `r pv(res[["FIEVRE TYPHOIDE"]]$principal$p_holm)` for typhoid fever and `r pv(res[["DIARRHEE DHY M5"]]$principal$p_holm)` for diarrhoea with dehydration. Effects grew over the first three months (figure 3): the lowest bin was `r sprintf("%.2f", effet_pic("IRA")$rrr)` for acute respiratory infection (weeks `r effet_pic("IRA")$sem_deb`–`r effet_pic("IRA")$sem_fin`) and `r sprintf("%.2f", effet_pic("FIEVRE TYPHOIDE")$rrr)` for typhoid fever (weeks `r effet_pic("FIEVRE TYPHOIDE")$sem_deb`–`r effet_pic("FIEVRE TYPHOIDE")$sem_fin`); typhoid fever then returned towards 1 by the final bin (`r sprintf("%.2f", tail(res[["FIEVRE TYPHOIDE"]]$evenement$table$rrr, 1))`).

## Robustness

The evidence differed by outcome. For acute respiratory infection the pre-trend test (*P*=`r pv(res[["IRA"]]$evenement$p_pre)`) and placebo (`r cip(sens("IRA", PLACEBO))`) gave no sign of differential prior trends, and the association persisted with zone-specific trends (`r cip(sens("IRA", TREND))`). For suspected malaria the placebo excluded 1 (`r cip(sens("PALUDISME SUSP", PLACEBO))`), showing a differential decline before the outbreak, so the main estimate is likely overstated; with zone-specific trends it attenuated to `r cip(sens("PALUDISME SUSP", TREND))`. For pneumonia the association was no longer distinguishable from the null with zone-specific trends (`r cip(sens("PNEUMONIE", TREND))`). These trend models also absorb part of a gradually developing effect, so they are conservative. Estimates changed little under alternative duplicate rules (appendix). Exposure definition mattered for pneumonia, whose association was imprecise with surveillance-based exposure (`r cip(sens("PNEUMONIE", "Exposure: IDS haemorrhagic fever incidence"))`). Excluding the two highest-burden zones strengthened the association for diarrhoea with dehydration (`r cip(sens("DIARRHEE DHY M5", "Excluding two highest-burden zones"))`), so this outcome should be regarded as uncertain rather than null. Removing one zone at a time gave RRRs for acute respiratory infection between `r sprintf("%.2f", res[["IRA"]]$sensibilite$loo[1])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", res[["IRA"]]$sensibilite$loo[2])`. The negative binomial mixed model gave similar estimates (`r cip(res[["IRA"]]$gamm$contraste)` for acute respiratory infection). In categorical analyses, associations were concentrated in zones with at least 50 EVD cases (appendix).

Among zones with valid confirmation data, confirmed malaria had an RRR of `r cip(res[["PALUDISME CONF"]]$principal)`, conditional on the exclusion rule. The odds ratio for the confirmed-to-suspected ratio was `r cip(R$positivite)`, so there was no clear evidence that this ratio changed with EVD burden once zones with loss of confirmation were excluded. Routine acute haemorrhagic fever notifications correlated only moderately with confirmed EVD cases by zone (Spearman ρ=`r sprintf("%.2f", R$concordance$rho)`).

# Discussion

In this province-wide analysis, zones with more confirmed EVD had larger relative falls in notifications of several common syndromes, starting around the outbreak declaration and largest in its first three months. Taken together with the literature from West Africa [@brolin2016; @elston2017], a fall across unrelated syndromes is more suggestive of a shared cause in access to, use of, or reporting from health services than of parallel falls in disease incidence. Our data cannot separate those mechanisms, and the distinction matters: fewer visits imply unmet need and possibly excess mortality [@walker2015; @parpia2016], whereas fewer reports may not.

The second finding is methodological and has immediate operational value. Most of the apparent province-wide fall in malaria positivity came from abrupt loss of confirmation in a subset of zones, several without EVD. Read at face value, as routine reports do, this looks like a fall in malaria transmission. If it reflects test stock-outs, patients may be receiving presumptive or no treatment during the peak of an emergency. Stock records could resolve this quickly.

## Limitations

First, there is no pre-outbreak year in the dataset. Week effects remove shared seasonality, but if season differs between zones in a way correlated with EVD burden, which is plausible given the province's geography, estimates would be confounded. The failed placebo for suspected malaria demonstrates that this is not hypothetical. Comparison with zone-level 2025 data is the most important next step. Second, exposure is measured once, during the post-period, and may partly reflect the capacity of zones to detect EVD; it cannot capture spatial spillover into neighbouring zones. Third, security events, displacement, and other interventions may correlate with EVD burden, and no such data were included. Fourth, population denominators were inconsistent in the source, and affect the incidence-based exposure, though not the fixed-effects outcome model. Fifth, syndromes are clinical notifications without laboratory confirmation, and the confirmed-malaria rule conditions on the outcome. Sixth, reporting completeness at health-area level was available for only a few zones. Finally, the analysis plan followed initial data exploration.

## Conclusions

Routine surveillance during the 2026 Ituri outbreak shows a burden-related fall in notified morbidity and a separate, potentially serious, loss of malaria confirmation. Both warrant verification with 2025 surveillance, facility utilisation, and test-stock data, and both argue for monitoring essential services as a standard part of Ebola response.
